intros.market: The WebPKI runs on 89 trusted CAs, but five organizations issue 92.4% of all certificates. Internet Security Research Group (Let's Encrypt) leads at 39.2%, followed by Google Trust Services at 20.9% and DigiCert at 15.3%. The remaining 75 CAs in the long tail collectively serve just 7.6% of issuance, creating a system where operational choices by a handful of entities dictate availability for the vast majority of the web.
intros.trust: Root program disagreement creates a fragmented trust landscape across 335 total roots. Only 38 CA owners appear in all four major stores, and just 90 individual roots enjoy universal trust. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, meaning chains that validate in Edge may fail elsewhere. This divergence forces CAs to maintain multiple hierarchies and complicates relying party validation logic across browsers.
intros.conc: Market concentration sits at HHI 2370, well above the 1800 threshold economists use to flag competitive concerns. The top three CAs control 75.5% of issuance, meaning a compliance failure or operational incident at any one could disrupt trust for three-quarters of the web. This systemic dependency amplifies the impact of the 1,566 incidents recorded across 54 CAs, where a single distrust event at a major issuer would cascade across billions of certificates.
intros.tail: Seventy-five CAs each issue less than 1% of certificates but retain full trust store inclusion, creating asymmetric risk exposure. These low-volume issuers face the same 6,664 regulatory obligations as the top five but lack comparable operational maturity or oversight attention. A governance failure in the tail may affect fewer certificates but still grants an attacker or incompetent operator the same universal trust as Let's Encrypt, as seen in the 16 distrust events where 10 involved patterns of repeated issues.
intros.geo: U.S.-incorporated CAs issue 91.95% of all certificates, with just 15 organizations dominating global issuance. Europe hosts 44 CAs but serves only 7.96% of volume, while Asia-Pacific's 17 CAs account for 0.09%. This geographic concentration means American corporate decisions and regulatory posture effectively govern trust for the global web, independent of where certificates are consumed or what legal frameworks apply in issuer jurisdictions.
intros.gov: Thirty government-operated or state-owned CAs hold trust store inclusion but issue only 0.07% of certificates. These entities pose unique risk because their operational incentives differ from commercial CAs and they may face competing loyalties between public trust requirements and state interests. Five jurisdictions on the high-risk list (China, Russia, United Kingdom, Australia, Hong Kong) operate CAs capable of issuing trusted certificates for any domain, creating surveillance and compelled access vectors regardless of low issuance volume.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions present high legal risk for compelled disclosure or lawful interception: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey occupy a moderate-risk tier. CAs incorporated in these countries operate under frameworks that may require assistance with surveillance, key escrow, or disclosure orders, creating tension with browser security policies that assume CAs resist government pressure. This risk layer intersects with the 30 government-operated CAs, some of which sit in these same high-risk legal environments.
intros.ops: The ecosystem has recorded 1,566 incidents across 54 CAs, with misissuance (609 cases) and governance failures (504 cases) leading the categories. CAs self-report only 26% of incidents, while external researchers, automated tools, and root programs collectively discover the majority. Policy and disclosure failures account for 194 and 139 incidents respectively, suggesting systemic issues in how CAs interpret requirements and communicate problems, patterns that feed the 16 distrust events where compliance and operational posture determined outcomes.
intros.crypto: Root certificate cryptographic posture spans legacy and modern algorithms, with key size and signature algorithm choices varying widely across the 335 trusted roots. The ecosystem continues transitioning from SHA-1 and 2048-bit RSA toward stronger primitives, but the pace remains uneven. Standards compliance gaps appear in audit findings, where 5 qualified opinions and 39 high-transparency-gap CAs suggest some organizations struggle to demonstrate adherence to cryptographic requirements, contributing to the broader operational risk profile.
intros.distrust: Sixteen distrust events have occurred across browser programs, with 14 involving compliance or operational failures and 10 showing patterns of repeated issues. Seven cases reflect negligent noncompliance, three involve demonstrated incompetence, and three show willful circumvention of requirements. The median runway from distrust announcement to enforcement is 1,185 days (over three years), meaning browsers tolerate long transition periods that may extend exposure to untrustworthy issuers well after problems surface.
intros.policy: Of 37 active TLS issuers measured, only 8 already operate at the 47-day maximum validity arriving in March 2029, while 5 still exceed the 100-day limit effective March 2027. Median current certificate lifetime is 67 days, showing many CAs remain unprepared for near-term validity reductions. This operational gap exists as the regulatory surface CAs navigate has grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6,664 total obligations (76% mandatory), with complexity expanding faster than CA maturity or the ecosystem's ability to detect non-compliance through audits that catch only 31% of in-scope incidents.
intros.governance: Root program oversight coverage has collapsed from 67.8% (Chrome) and 78.0% (Mozilla) in 2019 to 18.4% and 9.9% respectively in 2025, while Microsoft provides zero substantive review of the 223 incidents filed. Chrome commented substantively on 112 recent incidents across 730 bugs, Mozilla on 47 across 818 bugs, and Apple on 6 across 46 bugs. This decline means most incidents receive no authoritative interpretation or enforcement action, leaving CAs to self-assess compliance even as the regulatory surface expands to over 6,600 obligations.
intros.community: The CA/Browser Forum has 56 members but only 21 contribute actively, with 35 maintaining zero participation. Sectigo leads organizational engagement, while Stephen Davidson has proposed 36 ballots and endorsed 1. This silent majority pattern means a small group shapes policy for an ecosystem serving billions of users, and no new ballots have passed since 2022 despite the regulatory surface growing to 6,664 obligations, suggesting governance paralysis even as operational and compliance gaps widen.
intros.audit: Audit letters present a surveillance gap where 31% in-period detection rate means auditors caught only 129 of 414 in-scope incidents that later appeared in Bugzilla. Thirty-nine CAs show high transparency gaps between audit assertions and observed incident history, while 5 received qualified opinions. Only 9 CAs have adopted ETSI EN 319 411-1 v3.5, and 11 changed auditors in 2025. Self-reported findings appear in 59.2% of WebTrust letters and 66.4% of ETSI letters, but clean audit opinions routinely coexist with material compliance failures discovered months later, undermining audits as a primary oversight mechanism when root program coverage has fallen below 20%.
